title: Perform primary meat inspection incisions of small stock

lessons.title: Planning and preparing for small stock inspection
lessons.html:
Why small stock inspection is different

Sheep and goat lines run at high speed, and the carcasses are small. Inspection relies heavily on observation and palpation, with a limited number of routine incisions prescribed by the regulations under the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Additional incisions are made whenever observation or palpation reveals something abnormal.

Main targets

  • Liver fluke and other liver parasites.
  • Hydatid cysts and Cysticercus tenuicollis.
  • Sheep measles (Cysticercus ovis) in heart and muscles.
  • Caseous lymphadenitis in lymph nodes.
  • Pneumonia, lungworm and pleurisy.
  • Abscesses, bruising, emaciation, jaundice and contamination.

Preparing the station

  • Bright, even lighting at the head, pluck and carcass inspection points.
  • A pluck presentation system (hooks or trays) that keeps each pluck matched to its carcass.
  • Knife sterilizer at the correct temperature, and a hand-wash basin, within reach.
  • Two inspection knives, a steel and a hook.
  • Detention rail and tags; condemned containers.
  • PPE and clean protective clothing.

Planning

  1. Review ante-mortem findings, such as lame, thin or coughing animals, or animals from a farm with known problems.
  2. Confirm with the line supervisor how the line will be stopped or carcasses diverted.
  3. Check that the line speed allows a proper examination; report if it does not.

lessons.title: Performing the incisions on small stock
lessons.html:
Following the routine

Carry out the examination in a fixed order, using the prescribed observations, palpations and incisions you were trained in.

Head

  • Observe the head and mouth for lesions, such as scabby mouth or abscesses.
  • Palpate the head lymph nodes where required; incise if enlarged or abnormal.

Pluck

  • Lungs: observe and palpate both lungs for consolidation, nodules, cysts and adhesions. Palpate the bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes; incise if abnormal.
  • Heart: open the heart sac where required and observe the heart surface for Cysticercus ovis lesions. Incise the heart if routine or if lesions are suspected.
  • Liver: observe both surfaces and palpate. Incise the bile ducts on the visceral surface to check for liver fluke. Look for hydatid cysts and tenuicollis cysts.

Viscera

  • Observe the stomachs, intestines, spleen and mesenteric lymph nodes.

Carcass

  • Observe the outside and inside: pleura, peritoneum, diaphragm, kidneys.
  • Palpate the prescapular and prefemoral lymph nodes and other superficial nodes for enlargement, which may indicate caseous lymphadenitis. Incise abnormal nodes.
  • Look for bruises, abscesses, injection-site lesions, wool, faeces and ingesta.

Technique

  • Make clean, shallow, decisive cuts. Avoid unnecessary cuts, which reduce carcass value.
  • Sterilise the knife after each carcass and immediately after cutting a lesion, especially caseous lymphadenitis pus.
  • Keep pluck and carcass matched at all times.

lessons.title: Completing the inspection
lessons.html:
Deciding the next step

FindingAction
No abnormalityCarcass and organs continue to marking
Liver fluke or cysts in liver onlyRemove the affected liver to condemned; carcass continues if normal
Localised abscess or bruiseMark for trimming
Caseous lymphadenitis in several nodesDetain and refer
Cysticercus ovis lesionsDetain for further examination per the regulations
Signs of generalised diseaseDetain and refer

Making sure the action happens

  • Tag detained carcasses and their organs together.
  • Check that trimming is complete before the carcass is marked.
  • Ensure condemned parts go into marked, secure containers.

Records

Record carcass number, owner, findings, parts condemned, and detentions. Liver fluke and measles counts per producer are useful for farm feedback.

Speed and quality

On fast small stock lines there is pressure to rush. A missed lesion can reach consumers. If the line speed prevents proper inspection, the examiner must say so and the line must slow or stop. This is part of professional responsibility.

End of shift

  • Sterilise and store knives and hooks.
  • Clean the inspection stations.
  • Hand over records and report any outstanding detentions.

Key points

  • Small stock inspection relies mainly on observation and palpation, with prescribed incisions.
  • Incise the bile ducts to check for liver fluke; examine the heart for Cysticercus ovis.
  • Palpate superficial lymph nodes for caseous lymphadenitis.
  • Keep pluck and carcass matched and sterilise after each carcass and lesion.
  • Report when line speed does not allow proper inspection.

quiz.question: Small stock inspection relies mainly on which methods?

options.text: Observation and palpation, with prescribed incisions

quiz.question: Which incision is used to check for liver fluke in sheep?

options.text: Incising the bile ducts on the visceral surface

options.text: Say so; the line must slow or stop
